tier: ISP proxies, billed per IP by term

free_tier.stated: No free tier read on either page. The cheapest purchase is one address for 24 hours at $1.80; the same address costs $2.70 for 30 days, $2.55 for 60 days and $2.40 for 90 days. Included in every plan, in the vendor's words: 500K+ unique IPs in 31+ countries, country, state and city-level targeting, SOCKS5 support, UDP and TCP connections, IP replacement, unlimited sessions.
free_tier.notes: The 24-hour tier is the cheapest way to test one per-address ISP claim for a day. It is not a trial: it is the same product at its shortest term.

per_object_cap.notes: The unit sold is one IP address with a port, a username and a password, held for the term purchased.

retention.stated: not applicable: a rented address, not stored bytes
retention.notes: The only clock is the rental term, priced at 24 hours, 30, 60 and 90 days. The vendor describes the address as reserved for the buyer: Dedicated IP Pool, keep the same IP address as long as needed.

egress.terms: The same page states unlimited bandwidth and unlimited threads, and the buy page states unlimited sessions. Traffic is therefore not metered per byte, but the inclusion is qualified by a fair-use clause that publishes no number.
egress.free_allowance: traffic included with the per-IP price; no byte figure published and the fair-use clause is unquantified

interface_detail: The endpoint is a proxy address with a port, a username and a password, reachable over HTTP(S) or SOCKS5, which the page states as SOCKS5 support and UDP and TCP connections. The vendor also runs a self-service dashboard and refers to API access without publishing an endpoint on the two pages read. The schema's interface enum carries no proxy-protocol token, so rest indexes the dashboard and API only; the proxy protocol itself is stated here.
tooling: Any client that takes a proxy address with credentials: curl --proxy, Python requests with proxies=, a headless browser with proxy settings, or a SOCKS5-capable client. The vendor states a self-service dashboard and API access for pool management. No wrapper is needed; what the client would have to write is the check, a whois or RIPE lookup on the issued address confirming its registration before the class claim is relied on.
chaining: One purchased address in front of the outbound leg of the client's Workers AI gateway or crawler, where a stable per-request source address matters; it carries no storage and no compute, so it sits beside the compute and egress records rather than replacing either.

limits.value: no published request-rate or concurrency figure; the vendor states unlimited threads and unlimited sessions
one dedicated address per purchased slot, so all of a slot's traffic shares one IP's reputation; the vendor sells IP replacement as the remedy

limits_note: Zero session limits is prose naming no vocabulary kind: it says the vendor caps neither session length nor session count, which removes a shaping constraint rather than creating one. The fair-use clause behind included traffic is the one qualifier that could become a ceiling, and it publishes no number.
binding_note: The client's 45 GB a month across about 599,000 requests averages about 75,000 bytes and about 0.23 requests per second, and the vendor states unlimited sessions and unlimited threads with traffic included, so no rate, count or byte ceiling in the vocabulary is reachable; what does arrive first is money per address and the unquantified fair-use clause.

identity_cost.detail: A card is required to buy: Visa, Mastercard, PayPal, Alipay or crypto. No free tier and no anonymous purchase path was read. The buy page adds that the vendor limits abuse and gets to know customers before providing full access, so a paid order can still be gated on the vendor's own review.

reliability_note: One dedicated address carries all of a slot's traffic, so a block follows the address and the vendor's stated remedy is IP replacement; uptime is stated at 99.9% and success rate up to 99.99%, neither of which was measured here.
confidence_note: The quote, the feature text, the per-IP billing sentence and the fair-use qualifier were read on the two vendor pages on 2026-10-24. The price ladder and the payment methods are the research read of the same pricing page, passed on here: a raw fetch of that page by this record's author the same day returned the feature text and no dollar figures, because the price widget renders client-side. Measured would need one purchased address, a whois or RIPE lookup confirming its registration class, and a byte and request count through it.

evidence.proved: The FAQ, read directly: ISP proxies use IP addresses registered to consumer internet service providers. These IPs are hosted on data center servers. The same page states every ISP proxy belongs only to you, unlimited sessions, 500K+ unique IPs in 31+ countries, country/state/city targeting, SOCKS5 support, UDP and TCP, IP replacement, 99.9% uptime and a self-service dashboard.
Same page: unlimited threads, unlimited bandwidth claimed, and the FAQ answer giving an IP address, port, username and password as what the buyer receives.

The price ladder and payment methods as recorded by the research pass of 2026-10-24: $1.80 per proxy for 24 hours, $2.70 for 30 days, $2.55 for 60 days, $2.40 for 90 days; Visa, Mastercard, PayPal, Alipay or crypto. Passed on from that read, not re-observed by this record's raw fetch, which returned no dollar figures.

price_per_tb_month: no per-TB figure exists: the vendor bills per IP with traffic included. The comparable numbers are $1.80 per address per 24 hours, $2.70 per address per 30 days, $2.55 at 60 days and $2.40 at 90 days.
notes: The caveat is the class claim, not the price. Three routes were considered for checking it before purchase: (1) a published sample address, which neither page carries, so it is refuted; (2) a free trial, which does not exist, which is why the 24-hour tier at $1.80 is the cheapest way to make the claim checkable at all; (3) a published list of the hosting ASNs or prefixes, which the vendor does not publish. So an address's registration class cannot be inspected before money changes hands, and one $1.80 address plus a whois or RIPE lookup is what would settle it. and treating this as a storage product, since no per-object cap or retention applies to an address. One sample caveat: everything here rests on two vendor pages and no purchased address, so nothing about an issued IP was observed. CORRECTION to dossier/debrid/iproyal.json, which is named here because that record reads the same vendor: it carries the $1.80 headline as a monthly rate, in price_per_tb_month and in chaining, but $1.80 is the 24-hour tier and the 30-day price is $2.70, so that record understates a month by about a third. The same file's limits_note says a byte meter would have to be a fair-use clause and none was read; the pricing page read today carries exactly that clause, so the sentence is now stale. Neither file was edited by this record. Also noted: the interface vocabulary in this record's brief (socks5, http-proxy, api, web-ui) is not the enum in scripts/dossier/schema.json, which has no proxy token, so the array says rest and the protocol lives in interface_detail; extending that enum would stop the next proxy record from making the same compromise.
